tag.name: voice
tag.description: Both halves of a spoken conversation, for testing voice interfaces. **Say**: text with [tags] for emotion, pace and pauses becomes audio, stored by content so every request can be replayed byte for byte; replay stored audio, pin it under a key, or keep a human recording beside it. **Listen**: audio from the system under test becomes words, with find and compare to assert on what was said whatever its spelling, case or way of writing a number. Speech is Amazon Polly (each response says how faithfully each tag was rendered); listening is Amazon Transcribe.

get.summary: Say text: text (with [tags]) to audio, stored by content
get.description:
Turns text into spoken audio, and stores it by content.

**Replay.** The whole request (words, tags, voice, engine, format, sample rate, pronunciations) is reduced to a canonical form and hashed; the hash is `ref` and the audio is stored under it. The same request returns the same audio byte for byte with `cached: true` and nothing is synthesised, so a failing test can be run again on exactly the stimulus it failed on, and a thousand virtual users saying the same words cost one synthesis. Generated audio is kept 30 days after its last use; `voice/save` keeps one for good.

**Tags.** Put ElevenLabs-style tags in square brackets where the delivery should change: `[anxious] I've been waiting. [pause] Is the doctor late?`. Emotions (`[anxious]`, `[angry]`, `[sad]`, `[relaxed]`, ...), pace (`[slowly]`, `[quickly]`), volume (`[softly]`, `[loudly]`, `[whispers]`), pauses (`[pause]`, `[long pause]`, `[pause 800ms]`) and sounds (`[sighs]`, `[laughs]`). A tag holds until the next tag of its kind; `[neutral]` clears them. Tags are never spoken. `voice/tags` lists them all.

**Honest rendering.** No AWS voice takes emotion as an instruction today. Each tag is rendered as well as the chosen engine can and reported in `tags[]`: `native`, `approximated` (a change of rate, pitch or volume), `inferred` (generative voices read emotion from the wording) or `none` (not audible; sounds such as `[sighs]`). With `strict=true` a request with any `none` tag is refused with 422 before anything is synthesised. `ssml` shows exactly what the engine was asked to say.

**The audio** comes back as base64 in `data`; `url=true` gives a presigned URL instead; `view=true` or `download=true` redirect to the audio, so the say URL itself works as an `<audio src>`; `play=true` returns a small page that plays it from script with no player on screen (and one Play button if the browser will not let a page make sound before a click). `format=wav&hz=16000` is the form microphones and speech-to-speech streams take; in `wav` and `pcm`, a pause at the very start or end is exact digital silence.

**POST** takes the same names as a JSON body, plus `segments` (each `{"text", "emotion"}` or `{"pause": ms}`, each starting from the utterance's own emotion) and `pronounce` (`{"word": "how to say it"}`). A form body (`curl -d 'text=...'`) is read as fields; any other body is taken as the text. A `text` that is a complete `<speak>` document is passed to the engine as written.

**Say it again.** `ref` (or the `key` of a saved utterance) in place of `text` says the stored script again with another `voice`, `engine`, `format` or `hz` - a new ref, the same words and direction.

New synthesis is capped per day on each deployment (429 with `budgetExhausted` when used up); stored audio is never affected.

get.summary: Listen to stored audio: the words in an utterance, a saved recording or an earlier listening
get.description:
Turns audio into the words spoken in it: the other half of a spoken conversation. `voice/say` asks the question, the system under test answers in audio, and `voice/listen` tells the test what it said.

**The audio.** POST it as the request body, one of four ways: raw bytes with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`; the base64 of it as text; JSON `{"audio": "<base64>"}`; or JSON `{"chunks": ["<base64>", ...]}` - the pieces a speech-to-speech model streamed back, joined in the order given. Or name audio that is already stored: `ref` (an utterance from voice/say, or an earlier listening) or `key` (saved with voice/save). Up to 4096 KB.

**What can be listened to.** WAV (uncompressed, 8-48 kHz, mono or stereo), MP3, and audio with no header when you say what it is: `format=pcm&hz=24000` (16-bit mono little-endian samples - what Amazon Nova Sonic and most speech models emit), `format=mulaw` or `format=alaw` (telephone audio, 8000 Hz unless `hz` says otherwise). Ogg, FLAC, WebM, M4A and AMR uploads are refused with a 400: transcription is billed by the second, and only audio whose length can be counted from its bytes is passed on (convert to 16-bit WAV first). get.summary: Was this said? Search what was heard: words, a regex, or between two markers
get.description:
Was this said? Searches what was heard in audio - on normalised words, not on the written transcript, so an assertion does not break on spelling, case, punctuation or the way a number was written: `text=Tuesday the twenty-fourth at 3 pm` finds "Tuesday the 24th at 3 p.m.".

Name the audio with `ref` (from voice/listen or voice/say) or `key` - or POST it exactly as for voice/listen, and one request both listens and searches.

**Three ways to search** (choose one), as in mail/attachments/find:

* `text` (or `text64`): these words, in this order. `fuzzy=true` also accepts words spelt nearly the same (similarity 0.8; `fuzzy=0.6` sets it yourself); a number is never "nearly" right.
* `regex` (or `regex64`): a pattern, run on `normalised` and ignoring case - so `(\d+) pm` works however the time was written. `values` holds group 1 of each match, or the whole match.
* `left` + optional `right`: what was said between two markers. `left=reference number is` captures the number. Without `right` the capture runs to the end of the sentence. `values` holds the captures, as heard.

`exact=true` (with `text` or `regex`) searches the transcript as it was written instead - capitals, punctuation and all; `ignorecase=true` then relaxes the case.

**Each result** is given in the words heard: `matched`, `context` (the match with `context` words either side), `word` (its position, from 1), `startMs`/`endMs` (when it was said - how long the caller waited for it) and `confidence` (the least certain word in it).

**On a miss** (`found: false`) look at `closest`, the stretch heard that was most like what you asked for, and at `hint`. A name the transcriber misheard ("Newin" for "Nguyen") shows up here; `fuzzy` measures spelling, not sound, so for such names assert on something else in the sentence, or use a regex with the spellings you accept.

`wait` and `pending` work as in voice/listen: while the words are not ready the answer is 200 with `pending: true`, `found: null` and `count: null`; send the request again with the `ref` it returned.

get.summary: How close is what was heard to what was expected? Similarity, word error rate, differences
get.description:
How close is what was heard to what was expected? Compares word by word, on normalised words, and returns `similarity` (1 = the same words), `wordErrorRate` (the standard measure: substituted + missing + extra words, divided by the number of expected words) and `differences` - each place the two differ: what was expected, what was heard, where and when.

* `text` (or `text64`): what you expected to hear. `min=0.9` adds `pass`: true when `similarity` is at least that. For a reply whose wording changes from run to run, assert on the facts with voice/find instead.
* No `text`, and `ref` names an utterance made by voice/say (v...): a **round trip**. The utterance is listened to and compared with its own words (`roundTrip: true`). Use it to check that an utterance is intelligible before blaming the system under test for mishearing it.
* `otherref` / `otherkey`: compare with other audio - the words of an utterance, or what was heard in another recording (a baseline kept with voice/save).

The audio is named (`ref`, `key`) or POSTed as for voice/listen, and `wait` and `pending` work the same way: `same`, `similarity` and `wordErrorRate` are null while pending.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The audio heard: a listening (h...) from voice/listen, or an utterance (v...) from voice/say. Send ref or key, or POST the audio.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Saved audio (voice/save) as the audio heard.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Only for audio with no header: pcm (16-bit mono little-endian samples; hz is then required), mulaw or alaw (telephone audio). Leave it out for WAV and MP3.

parameters.name: hz
parameters.description: Sample rate of headerless audio, 8000-48000. Required with format=pcm (Amazon Nova Sonic emits 24000); mulaw and alaw default to 8000.

parameters.name: language
parameters.description: The language to listen for: an Amazon Transcribe code such as en-AU, en-US or en-GB, or auto to identify it. Default: the deployment's language (en-AU).

parameters.name: wait
parameters.description: Seconds to hold the request while the audio is transcribed, 0-20. Default 20. If the words are not ready in time the answer is 200 with pending: true.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: What you expected to hear. Send text, otherref or otherkey - or none of them for a round trip of an utterance.
parameters.example: Your next appointment is on Tuesday the 24th at 3 pm with Dr Nguyen

parameters.name: text64
parameters.description: Base64 of text.

parameters.name: otherref
parameters.description: Compare with this audio instead of text: an utterance (v..., its words) or a listening (h..., what was heard).

parameters.name: otherkey
parameters.description: Compare with this saved audio instead of text.

parameters.name: min
parameters.description: A similarity from 0 to 1. Adds pass: true when similarity is at least this.
